hints: Think about what type of catalyst allows a chloroalkane to form a carbocation, consider how a strong Lewis acid can accept the chloride.
walkthrough:
Spot the Friedel-Crafts step**
You have benzene plus $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$ giving ethylbenzene. This is Friedel-Crafts alkylation. Benzene needs a strong electrophile, here $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5^+$, not the neutral chloroethane.

Bring in the Lewis acid**
The $\text{C-Cl}$ bond will not break on its own. A Lewis acid such as $\text{AlCl}_3$ (or $\text{FeCl}_3$) accepts the lone pair on Cl, polarising and breaking the bond to release $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5^+$ and form $\text{AlCl}_4^-$.
Final answer: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl} + \text{AlCl}_3 \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5^+ + \text{AlCl}_4^-$

hints: Recall the numbering of a benzene ring, 1,2 means adjacent carbons and 1,4 means opposite carbons.
walkthrough:
Draw the common backbone**
Start with a hexagon with a circle for benzene in both boxes. Each ethyl substituent is $-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$.

Place the groups correctly**
For 1,2, put the two ethyl groups on neighbouring carbons, side by side. For 1,4, put them on opposite sides of the ring, with one carbon gap on each side between them.

Final answer: 1,2-diethylbenzene: benzene ring with two $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ groups on adjacent carbons (ortho). 1,4-diethylbenzene: benzene ring with two $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ groups on opposite carbons (para).

hints: Think about the ethyl group already on ethylbenzene, is it electron donating or withdrawing and where does it direct the next electrophile?
walkthrough:
Remember the directing power of alkyl**
An alkyl group pushes electrons toward the ring by the positive inductive effect. This activates the ring and directs the incoming $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5^+$ to the 2, 4 and 6 positions, which are ortho and para to itself.

Link to the missing isomer**
Positions 2 and 6 give 1,2-diethylbenzene, position 4 gives 1,4-diethylbenzene. Position 3 and 5 would give 1,3-diethylbenzene (meta), which is not activated by the ethyl group, so very little forms.
Final answer: Ethyl group is electron donating by positive inductive effect and is 2,4-directing (ortho, para directing), so substitution at 3-position (meta) is disfavoured.

hints: Recall which vigorous oxidant converts alkyl side chains on benzene fully to $\text{COOH}$, think purple oxidant with heat and alkali.
walkthrough:
Recognise complete side chain oxidation**
Both $-\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$ groups are oxidised right down to $-\text{COOH}$ while the benzene ring survives. Only a very strong oxidant does this.

Name the standard reagent**
That reagent is hot alkaline potassium manganate(VII), $\text{KMnO}_4$, heated under reflux, then acidified to give the free diacid.
Final answer: Hot alkaline $\text{KMnO}_4$ / $\text{MnO}_4^-$, heat, followed by acidification.

hints: Write the formula of 1,2-diethylbenzene as $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{14}$ and note the product $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4(\text{COOH})_2$ is $\text{C}_8\text{H}_6\text{O}_4$, so carbon lost must appear as $\text{CO}_2$.
Balance C first, then H with $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, then O with [O] to find how many [O] atoms are needed.
walkthrough:
Write all correct formulae**
1,2-diethylbenzene is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2 = \text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{14}$. The diacid is $\text{C}_8\text{H}_6\text{O}_4$. Since all atoms in the ethyl groups are fully oxidised, extra carbon forms $\text{CO}_2$ and extra hydrogen forms $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Balance atoms**
C: $10$ on left, $8$ in diacid, so need $2\text{CO}_2$. H: $14$ on left, $6$ in diacid, so need $4\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to give $6 + 8 = 14$. O: right side has $4 + 4 + 4 = 12$ O atoms, so need $$\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{14} + 12[\text{O}] \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_4(\text{COOH})_2 + 2\text{CO}_2 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

hints: Look for symmetry in benzene-1,2-dioic acid, which ring carbons are mirror images of each other when the two $\text{COOH}$ groups are identical?
walkthrough:
Find equivalent carbons**
Benzene-1,2-dioic acid has a plane of symmetry through the middle of the 1-2 bond and the 4-5 bond. So C1 = C2, C3 = C6, C4 = C5, and the two $\text{C=O}$ carbons are identical.

Count environments**
That gives three different ring carbon environments plus one carbonyl carbon environment, total 4 distinct $^{13}\text{C}$ environments, so 4 peaks.

hints: Compare $\text{CHCl}_3$ which contains $^1\text{H}$ with $\text{CDCl}_3$ which contains D, think about which nucleus the spectrometer detects.
walkthrough:
Why normal solvent is a problem**
$^1\text{H}$ NMR detects protons. If you dissolve in $\text{CHCl}_3$, the huge number of solvent $\text{H}$ atoms would give a giant peak that swamps the sample peaks.

Why deuteration solves it**
In $\text{CDCl}_3$ the H is replaced by deuterium, $^2\text{H}$, which resonates at a different frequency and is invisible in the $^1\text{H}$ spectrum, leaving only sample peaks.
Final answer: $\text{CDCl}_3$ contains no $^1\text{H}$ (D is not detected in $^1\text{H}$ NMR) so it gives no peak and does not interfere with the spectrum.

hints: Compare Fig. 6.1 with three groups of peaks and Fig. 6.2 with only two peaks, which molecule has an ethyl group that would show splitting?
Recall the n+1 rule, a $\text{CH}_3$ next to $\text{CH}_2$ is split by 2 protons, and a $\text{CH}_2$ next to $\text{CH}_3$ is split by 3 protons.
Match chemical shifts, the $\text{CH}_3$ further from the ring appears near $\delta$ 1.2 and the benzylic $\text{CH}_2$ nearer the ring appears near $\delta$ 2.6.
walkthrough:
Identify Fig. 6.1 as ethylbenzene**
Fig. 6.1 shows a multiplet near $\delta$ 7.2 for the phenyl protons, plus two aliphatic signals at $\delta$ 1.2 and 2.6. That fits $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Fig. 6.2 has only aromatic and highly deshielded acid protons, so it must be the diacid.

Assign the triplet at 1.2**
The $\delta$ 1.2 signal is the $\text{CH}_3$ group. Its neighbours are the 2 protons of the $\text{CH}_2$. By the n+1 rule, $$n+1 = 2+1 = 3$$ so it appears as a triplet.

Assign the quartet at 2.6**
The $\delta$ 2.6 signal is the benzylic $\text{CH}_2$ group, deshielded by the ring. Its neighbours are the 3 protons of the $\text{CH}_3$. So $$n+1 = 3+1 = 4$$ giving a quartet.

Final answer: substance: ethylbenzene, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$ (Fig. 6.1).
peak at $\delta$ = 1.2: triplet, $\text{CH}_3$, split by 2H on neighbouring C / next to $\text{CH}_2$.
peak at $\delta$ = 2.6: quartet, $\text{CH}_2$, split by 3H on neighbouring C / next to $\text{CH}_3$.

hints: Fig. 6.2 shows only two singlets, one near $\delta$ 7.8 and one very downfield near $\delta$ 13.1, think which protons in $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4(\text{COOH})_2$ are aromatic and which are highly deshielded.
walkthrough:
Confirm the molecule**
By elimination Fig. 6.2 must be benzene-1,2-dioic acid. It has no alkyl protons, so no signals at $\delta$ 1 to 3, which matches.

Assign both peaks**
The sharp peak at $\delta$ 7.8 is in the aromatic region, due to the four ring protons on $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4$. The broad peak at $\delta$ 13.1 is very deshielded, characteristic of the $\text{O-H}$ proton in $\text{COOH}$.

Final answer: substance: benzene-1,2-dioic acid, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4(\text{COOH})_2$.
peak at $\delta$ = 7.8: H on benzene / $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4$. peak at $\delta$ = 13.1: $\text{COOH}$ / carboxylic acid proton.

hints: Think about what happens to an $\text{O-H}$ proton when shaken with $\text{D}_2\text{O}$, is it exchangeable?
walkthrough:
Spot the labile proton**
The $\text{COOH}$ proton is acidic and labile. In $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ it rapidly exchanges: $$\text{RCOOH} + \text{D}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{RCOOD} + \text{HOD}$$

Explain the missing signal**
Deuterium does not appear in a $^1\text{H}$ spectrum, so the $\delta$ 13.1 peak vanishes, while the aromatic $\text{C-H}$ protons do not exchange and remain.

Final answer: Peak at $\delta$ 13.1 ($\text{COOH}$) disappears as the acidic proton exchanges with deuterium / D from $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ to give $\text{COOD}$, which is not seen in $^1\text{H}$ NMR.

hints: Look at what is lost when two adjacent $\text{COOH}$ groups form the cyclic product K, count the atoms of the small molecule removed.
walkthrough:
Track the atoms lost**
Two $-\text{COOH}$ groups join to give $-\text{CO-O-CO-}$ plus $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. No other reagent is involved, just heat.

Name the type**
Loss of water from one molecule to form a ring is intramolecular dehydration, also called condensation or elimination to form an acid anhydride.
Final answer: Dehydration / elimination / condensation (formation of cyclic anhydride with loss of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$).
